abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel cognitive-inspired framework for speech perception modeling that fundamentally reconceptualizes how prosodic information interacts with lexical processing in spoken language understanding. Unlike conventional models that treat prosody as auxiliary acoustic cues, the proposed Cognitive Prosodic Integration (CPI) theory posits a bidirectional coupling mechanism where rhythmic patterns actively shape lexical access through predictive coding principles. We formulate mathematical descriptions of the interaction between hierarchical prosodic structures (intonational phrases, prosodic words, syllables) and phonological representations, establishing differential equations that capture the temporal dynamics of perception. The theoretical analysis demonstrates that this framework naturally accounts for phenomena including pitch accent assignment asymmetries, boundary-related lengthening effects, and speech perception adaptation under degraded acoustic conditions. Critically, the model generates testable predictions regarding neural correlates of prosodic processing that distinguish it from existing accounts. Simulation experiments validate the theoretical predictions across multiple corpora spanning phonetically controlled laboratory speech and naturally occurring conversational data. This paradigm shift from additive feature integration to dynamic predictive coupling offers a new theoretical foundation for spoken language processing research, with implications for both speech technology applications and cognitive science investigations of human speech perception.

This paper presents a substantially refined theoretical analysis of neural network architectures for automatic speech recognition, addressing critical limitations in existing end-to-end modeling approaches regarding their ability to capture long-range contextual dependencies and their theoretical interpretability. We extend the contemporary attention-based sequence-to-sequence framework by introducing hierarchical temporal aggregation mechanisms that operate across multiple time scales, enabling more effective modeling of both fine-grained phonetic details and broader discourse-level coherence. The theoretical contribution includes a rigorous mathematical characterization of how gradient propagation behaves differently across hierarchical attention layers, providing insights into why certain architectural configurations fail to generalize on extended utterances. We derive theoretical bounds on the sample complexity required for training such architectures under non-stationary acoustic conditions, demonstrating that the proposed hierarchical structure reduces the theoretical sample complexity by a factor proportional to the number of aggregation levels. Experimental validation on benchmark speech recognition corpora confirms that the architectural improvements yield consistent word error rate reductions across diverse acoustic environments. This work provides both a theoretical foundation for understanding deep learning in speech processing and practical architectural guidelines for building more robust speech recognition systems.

This paper presents a revolutionary multi-modal dialogue system architecture that fundamentally transforms human-computer speech interaction by unifying speech recognition, natural language understanding, and speech synthesis into a single differentiable neural pipeline. The proposed Integrated Conversational Architecture (ICA) eliminates traditional pipeline boundaries by employing a shared latent representation space that simultaneously encodes linguistic meaning, paralinguistic information, and speaker characteristics. The system architecture incorporates a novel cross-modal attention mechanism that enables real-time bidirectional information flow between speech analysis and generation components, allowing the system to maintain consistent voice identity while dynamically adapting prosodic style to conversational context. We detail the complete engineering pipeline including data collection protocols, training procedures, and inference optimization strategies necessary for deploying the system in real-time interaction scenarios. Extensive evaluation demonstrates that ICA achieves unprecedented coherence scores in extended conversations, with users rating the naturalness and personality consistency significantly higher than conventional modular systems. The system's ability to perform real-time voice conversion while maintaining conversational coherence represents a paradigm shift in dialogue system design, opening new possibilities for accessible speech technology applications.

This paper describes a significantly enhanced speech enhancement system designed for real-time operation in challenging acoustic environments with multiple competing talkers and substantial background noise. The proposed architecture advances existing neural network-based speech enhancement through a novel two-stage processing pipeline that separates speech denoising from speaker separation using carefully designed recurrent memory mechanisms. The first stage employs a frequency-domain convolutional network with learned filter banks optimized for speech quality preservation, while the second stage utilizes a speaker-aware separation module that leverages speaker embedding representations to discriminate between simultaneous talkers. We introduce substantial engineering innovations including a new training curriculum that progressively increases acoustic complexity, a lightweight model compression approach achieving 70% parameter reduction with minimal performance degradation, and a streaming inference implementation enabling sub-10ms latency processing. Extensive benchmarking on standardized speech enhancement datasets demonstrates that the system achieves state-of-the-art scores on both objective speech quality metrics and automatic speech recognition accuracy in enhanced conditions. The practical deployment considerations, including memory footprint analysis and computational complexity evaluation, make this system suitable for integration into mobile devices and hearing assistive technologies.
